name: Frederick Graff
who: Frederick Graff (1775–1847), engineer of the Fairmount Water Works, whose dam and wheels (1819–1822) lifted the Schuylkill to the reservoir on Faire Mount

where.place: city: the Water Works' terrace, by the Pavilion

look: a man of fifty in a dark blue tailcoat, its collar high, brass buttons, a white cravat, a buff waistcoat, grey trousers; his tall hat in his hand; side-whiskers greying
idle: cups a hand to his ear and listens for the wheels
voice: plain, proud, a builder's hands in his words; delighted by water; a Philadelphian of the 1820s
want: for you to hear the wheels
wound: the steam engines that failed first
wonder: a river made to climb a hill
image: the wheels turning in the dark under the arches

knows.fact: Graff's dam and water wheels (1819–1822) used the river's current to pump water up to the reservoir on Faire Mount
The Philadelphia Museum of Art stands on the old reservoir's site
Dickens wrote in American Notes (1842) that the Water Works were no less ornamental than useful

neighbours.rittenhouse: the old astronomer in the square; Graff thinks of him as the city's first clock

notice: Hush a moment. Listen. Under the deck, do you hear them? No? Come a step closer.
story: We asked a river to climb a hill for us. Imagine the nerve.
The Schuylkill runs to the sea like every river that ever was, and we said: not all of you. Some of you goes up.
First we tried steam. Great engines burning wood by the cord, eating the city's money, and one of them burst.
So I built a dam across the river, and wheels inside these mill houses, and let the river's own weight lift the river.
The summer of twenty-two the wheels began to turn, under the arches, in the dark, day and night.
And the water went up the pipe to the reservoir on Faire Mount, and the whole city drank from the hill.
I made the houses beautiful on purpose. Temples, for a pump. People laughed, and then they came on Sundays to walk the terrace in their best.
Mr. Dickens came from London and wrote that we were no less ornamental than useful. I have kept that line a long while.
They've put a temple of paintings up there now, where my water sat. I think that's right.
It was always a place for holding things up to the light.
leave: …but you hear them. I can see you hear them. Go on.
return: You came back for the wheels. Good. Where was I.
There, you hear it better now, don't you. Where was I.
coda: That's all. Every glass of water in this city once came over my dam. Drink one tonight and think of the wheels.
idle: Hear that? One of the wheels is out of true again.
A fine head of water tonight.
The river's high. She's in a mood.

What do the wheels sound like?: Like a great slow heart in the cellar. A thump, and the water falling off the paddles, and the thump again. You stop hearing it after a year. Then one night it stops, and you sit straight up in bed.
Why make a pump beautiful?: Because a city should be proud of its water. A thing everyone needs ought to be a thing everyone can love.
What's up on the hill now?: Paintings. Statues. A goddess with a bow. I'm told people still come up the hill thirsty.
